Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 523 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018) 
 
 
Background 
Kimiwan-Winagami Lakes Wildlife Management Unit 523 (WMU 523) in the Peace Region, covers an area of 
5,680.9 km2, with 386 km2 designated as a Key Wildlife and Biodiversity Zone and includes Greene-Valley 
Provincial Park (44.6 km2). The WMU also has a Road Corridor Wildlife Sanctuary on Secondary Road 986 and 
the Peace River Pulp Road C. The boreal dry mixedwood forest is the predominant subregion in the WMU, with a 
smaller portion of the boreal central mixedwood occurring along the eastern boundary. The WMU is dominated by 
agriculture and is primarily deeded land with some Crown land along the river valley and WMU boundaries. First 
Nations reserves present in WMU 523 include William McKenzie (No.151K), Kapawe’no  (No. 150B, 150C, 150D, 
229), and Sucker Creek (No. 150A). 
A survey for ungulates (moose, mule deer and white-tailed deer) was last conducted for WMU 523 in 2011 using 
the random stratified block methodology (Random Block). See Table 2 for previous ungulate survey estimates for 
WMU 523. 
The objective of the 2018 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 523 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density and the age-sex composition. 
 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted from January 19th to 23rd, 2018 using distance sampling techniques 
(Buckland et al., 2001, 2010). A total of 189 north-south transect lines (survey effort = 1,020 km) were flown. WMU 
523 was divided into three strata: agricultural land (3,666.8 km2), river valley (1,528.0 km2 and deciduous-
mixedwood forest (486.1 km2). Ungulates were classified by age class (adult or calf) and sex. Other wildlife 
sightings were recorded. A density estimate for elk was  not attempted due to limited observations. 
 
Results 
Moose 
A total of 254 moose were observed in 154 groups. The estimated density was 0.42 moose/km2 (90% CI 0.33 – 
0.54) and the estimated abundance was 2,379 individuals (90% CI 1,853 – 3,056). The coefficient of variation for 
both density and abundance was 0.15 (Table 3). A total of 242 moose were successfully classified and the 
bull:cow:calf ratio was estimated to be 25:100:55. The population appears to have decreased slightly since the last 
population estimate.

Mule Deer 
A total of 150 mule deer were observed in 39 groups. The estimated density was 0.28 deer/km2 (90% CI 0.13 – 
0.61) and the estimated abundance was 1,631 individuals (90% CI 769 – 3,459). The coefficient of variation for 
both density and abundance was 0.39 (Table 3). A total of 117 mule deer were successfully classified and the 
buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 42:100:83. 
 
White-tailed deer 
A total of 235 white-tailed deer were observed in 74 groups. The estimated density was 0.47 deer/km2 (90% CI 
0.35 – 0.65) and the estimated abundance was 2,690 individuals (90% CI 1,966 – 3,682).  The coefficient of 
variation for both density and abundance was 0.19 (Table 3). A total of 162 white-tailed deer were successfully 
classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 8:100:74. It should be noted that this ratio likely 
underestimates buck availability given the timing of the survey relative to antler drop.
